Resources identified by URIs using nouns (/users/42/orders), not verbs (/getOrders)
HTTP methods express the action (GET, POST, PUT/PATCH, DELETE); status codes express the outcome
Stateless: each request carries everything needed (e.g. an auth token); the server keeps no client session between requests
Other constraints: client-server, cacheable responses, uniform interface, layered system
Good practice: versioning (/api/v1), pagination and filtering via query parameters, consistent JSON error format
entries.referenceAnswer: REST is a style of designing APIs around resources. Each resource has a URL, the HTTP method says what to do with it, and the status code says how it went. Requests are stateless: each one carries its own authentication and context, so any server can handle it, which makes scaling easy. Responses can be cacheable. For users and orders I'd use GET /users/42 to fetch a user, PATCH /users/42 to update them, GET /users/42/orders to list their orders, with ?page=2&status=shipped for pagination and filtering, POST /users/42/orders to create one, and DELETE /orders/7 to cancel one. URLs contain nouns, not verbs like /createOrder. I'd return 201 on creation, 404 for missing resources and 400 for validation errors, in a consistent JSON error format, and version the API under /api/v1.
commonMistakes: Using verbs in URLs
Returning 200 for errors with an error message in the body

questions: What system calls are used to create a TCP server and a TCP client?
How can one server handle many clients at the same time?
keyPoints: Server: socket() creates the endpoint, bind() attaches it to an IP and port, listen() marks it as passive, accept() waits for and returns a NEW socket for each client
Client: socket(), then connect() to the server's IP and port (the OS picks an ephemeral local port)
Both then use send()/recv() (or read()/write()) and close()
The listening socket keeps accepting while each accepted socket handles one client
Many clients: a thread/process per client, a thread pool, or I/O multiplexing (select, poll, epoll) in an event loop, which is how Node.js and Nginx work
entries.referenceAnswer: A TCP server calls socket() to create an endpoint, bind() to attach it to an address and port, and listen() to start accepting connections. Then it loops on accept(), which blocks until a client connects and returns a brand new socket dedicated to that client, while the original socket keeps listening. The client just calls socket() and connect() with the server's address, and the OS picks an ephemeral port for it. After that both sides send and receive on their connected sockets and finally close them. To serve many clients at once, the classic approach is a thread or process per connection, or a pool of threads. High-performance servers like Nginx and Node.js use I/O multiplexing instead: a single event loop asks the OS, via epoll or similar, which sockets are ready, and handles each one without blocking.
commonMistakes: Thinking the server communicates through the listening socket
Forgetting bind() and listen() on the server

questions: What is a VPN and how does it work?
Does a VPN make you anonymous on the Internet?
keyPoints: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and a VPN server over the public Internet
Your traffic is encapsulated and encrypted, so the local network/ISP only sees encrypted traffic to the VPN server
Websites see the VPN server's IP address instead of yours
Uses: remote access to a company's private network, site-to-site links between offices, privacy on public Wi-Fi
Protocols: IPsec, OpenVPN, WireGuard
Not full anonymity: the VPN provider can see your traffic, and logins/cookies/browser fingerprinting still identify you
entries.referenceAnswer: A VPN builds an encrypted tunnel from your device to a VPN server. Your packets are wrapped and encrypted, sent to that server, unwrapped there, and forwarded to their real destination. So your local network or ISP sees only encrypted traffic going to one server, and websites see the VPN server's IP instead of yours. Companies use VPNs so employees can reach internal systems from home as if they were in the office, and to connect office networks site to site. Protocols include IPsec, OpenVPN and WireGuard. It doesn't make you anonymous, though: you've just shifted trust to the VPN provider, who can see your traffic, and websites can still identify you through logins, cookies and browser fingerprinting.
commonMistakes: Saying a VPN provides complete anonymity
Confusing a VPN with a VLAN

questions: What is the difference between SSH and Telnet?
How does SSH key-based authentication work?
keyPoints: Both provide remote command-line access to another machine
Telnet (port 23) sends everything, including passwords, in plain text; obsolete for remote login
SSH (port 22) encrypts the whole session and verifies the server's identity with a host key
Key-based auth: the public key is placed on the server (authorized_keys); the client proves it holds the matching private key by signing a challenge; the private key never leaves the client
SSH also supports secure file transfer (scp, sftp) and port forwarding/tunnelling
entries.referenceAnswer: Both give you a remote terminal, but Telnet sends everything in plain text, including your username and password, so anyone sniffing the network can read them. That's why it's essentially obsolete. SSH encrypts the entire session, and it also verifies the server using a host key, which is why you get a warning if a server's key suddenly changes. With key-based login, you put your public key in the server's authorized_keys file. When you connect, the server sends a challenge, and your client signs it with your private key, which never leaves your machine. The server verifies the signature with the public key. It's more secure than passwords and easy to automate. SSH also handles file copying with scp and sftp, and can tunnel other connections.
commonMistakes: Saying the private key is sent to the server
Mixing up the port numbers
